summary:
Kırşehir stands under Turkish state law. The sources document no statute, municipal ordinance, police practice or incident originating in Kırşehir itself; the national framework sets what a trans or LGBTQ visitor to the province can expect to face.

Homosexuality has not been a criminal offence in Turkey since the Ottoman Empire adopted a new penal code in 1858, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender, after surgery, since 1988. That decriminalisation does not amount to a rights framework: Turkey has no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, same-sex relationships receive no legal recognition covering marriage, civil union and adoption, and LGBTQ people are barred from serving openly in the military. In ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow Europe ranking Turkey placed 47th of 49 assessed countries.

Kaos GL's LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025, presented on 24 February 2026 under the title 'The Year of the Family: A Major Siege Against LGBTI+ People', finds that anti-LGBTI+ hostility became explicit state policy over the year. Targeting of LGBTI+ people as 'deviant' or 'a threat' by the president and senior officials raised officials' motivation and third-party impunity; the new Family Ministry became the implementing ministry; one LGBTI+ rights organisation was closed; platforms and broadcasters were penalised or withdrew; and artistic events were cancelled. The report documents six violations of the right to life, three of them hate-motivated killings, with trans people most affected, alongside 89 torture or ill-treatment violations against 51 the previous year, largely during assemblies, and 313 liberty violations, about 2.5 times the previous year and mostly detentions. No official hate-crime statistics exist in Turkey, so these cases rely on media reporting.

Identity checks on the street remain a live exposure point. In July 2025 bianet reported that about 20 trans women in Istanbul's Beyoğlu district were rounded up for identity checks at a police station, their names recorded and videos filmed, with no official reason given. Detainees are held in facilities organised by registered sex rather than gender identity, and Pride events have been banned in Istanbul and most other cities in most years since 2015, using tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions against participants.

Protection machinery is thin. Turkey has no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on sexual orientation or gender identity, and hormone replacement therapy is not covered by the government healthcare system, so a trans visitor who needs medication during a stay must obtain and pay for it privately.
tangentialFactors:
The 2025 reporting year sits within a broader pattern of state-led hostility rather than isolated prejudice: the Kaos GL report attributes the rise in detentions, ill-treatment and life violations directly to official rhetoric and to institutional measures such as the new Family Ministry and the closure of an LGBTI+ rights organisation.

Turkey's position near the bottom of ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow Europe ranking, 47th of 49, is consistent with the domestic picture documented by Kaos GL and bianet, and gives a comparative benchmark for the level of legal protection a visitor can rely on.
localsOnly:
Residents face a documented gap in legal protection: Turkey has no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on sexual orientation or gender identity, and no direct protection on gender identity grounds. Legal gender change has been available since 1988 but only after surgery.

LGBTQ people are barred from serving openly in the military, and same-sex relationships receive no legal recognition for marriage, civil union or adoption. One LGBTI+ rights organisation was closed during 2025, and platforms, broadcasters and artistic events faced penalties or cancellation under the same policy direction.

There are no official hate-crime statistics in Turkey; monitoring organisations compile cases from media reporting, which means the recorded figures understate the actual incidence.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the draft legislative package reported by Human Rights Watch in October 2025 has since been enacted is unresolved in the sources available for this record.

The source inventory contains no Kırşehir-specific statute, ordinance, police practice, incident or institution; the province-level assessment rests entirely on the national framework.

The Rainbow Europe source for Turkey yielded no usable finding beyond the ranking position cited, and no per-city or per-province breakdown of the 2025 violation counts is available, so the distribution of those cases across Kırşehir is not sourced.
